newsitem.title: BELARUS: Lukashenko offer does not end power struggle.
newsitem.headline: Lukashenko offer does not end power struggle.

text.p: Opponents of Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko on Sunday cautiously welcomed his offer of compromise over a controversial referendum but said a political battle over his attempts to broaden his powers were not over.

Lukashenko, accused of trying to build a dictatorship, on Saturday agreed to change the date of a referendum on extending his powers to November 24, the same day as a referendum proposed by parliament which could abolish the post of president.
He made the offer after thousands of people opposed to the 42-year-old leader marched through the streets of Minsk on Saturday to denounce him as a dictator and demand he resign.
"I think we are closer to achieving stability than we were two days ago," said communist Sergei Kolyakin, head of the largest faction in parliament.
Lukashenko had originally wanted to hold his referendum on November 7. Opponents saw some victory in his bowing to the constitution, which says parliament is the final arbiter.
"Lukashenko has not offered a real compromise. He simply understood he had to obey the law," Kolyakin told reporters. Other opposition figures echoed his comments.
But the fiery president, elected in 1994 on a platform of fighting crime and forming a closer union with Russia, accused deputies on Sunday of indulging in a "wild battle for power".

"Forget it if you are thinking that the president has shown weakness by compromising on the referendum date," he said in a speech to an "All-Belarus People's Congress" he convened to approve plans for his own referendum.
In speeches on Saturday and Sunday, the imposing, moustachioed Lukashenko railed at his opponents, demanding that they also make concessions.
Making clear the battle was not yet over, Communist Kolyakin said parliament would drop its referendum if Lukashenko also scrapped his.
If approved by voters, Lukashenko would have authority to appoint court judges, half the constitutional court and half the electoral commission.
Opposition parties, who have a majority in parliament, would expect Lukashenko to drop plans to extend his term, due to end in 1999, by more than two years, Kolyakin added.

Lukashenko's congress, strongly reminiscent of Soviet-era gatherings, passed a resolution by 4,942 to 11 with 47 abstensions urging parliament to drop its referendum questions and offering no further compromise itself.

Lukashenko, who called NATO a "dreadful monster" on the eve of commemorations of the Allied World War Two victory in May, has incensed nationalists by seeking a closer union with Russia and deriding the little-used Belarussian language.
Previous protests have ended with scores of arrests and dozens of people receiving short prison terms but Saturday's meeting passed off without major incident.
Lukashenko has come under fire from several international bodies, such as the European Union, which has urged both sides to find a compromise.
